title: Kangha: the small comb
hookLine: a small wooden comb, for keeping the hair clean and ordered

cards: Two gardens can grow from the same promise. In one, nothing is ever cut and nothing is ever tended: brambles everywhere, paths gone, beautiful in a wild way, but impossible to walk through.
In the other, nothing has been cut either, but every morning the gardener walks through, untangles, clears the paths, sweeps. Same plants. Completely different garden.
Uncut hair, in Sikh teaching, is meant to be the second garden. That's why, right in the kesh, Sikhs who keep the five Ks carry a small wooden comb.

teach.b: Kangha means comb. It's the second of the five Ks: a small comb, usually wooden, kept in the hair, often tucked into the knot under the turban. Its job is plain: to keep the kesh clean and ordered.
The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to comb their hair twice a day and tie the turban neatly. Why does such a small thing matter? Here's the usual explanation.
In the Gurus' time, some ascetics wore their hair long and matted as a sign that they had left the world behind. The Sikh Gurus honored devotion, but they didn't ask anyone to leave the world.
They taught householders to live in it: to work, marry, raise children, serve. So Sikhs keep their hair uncut, like the ascetics, and comb it, unlike the ascetics' matted locks.
The kangha says: devotion inside ordinary life, not away from it. Some Sikhs also read it inwardly.
Twice a day the comb pulls the tangles from the hair; twice a day the prayers do the same for the mind.
And there's a gentleness in it. A comb doesn't cut anything or fight the hair.

It just untangles, patiently, again tomorrow. That's the week, too: Farid's Creator in creation, the crows and the eyes, the Gurus answering Farid, the Bhagats still ahead, rehat, kesh, and now the kangha.
The saints showed what to love. The rehat shows how to live it, morning and evening, one tangle at a time.

games.q: in the Gurus' time, some ascetics wore long, matted hair to show they'd left the world. what does the kangha say instead?
o: keep the hair uncut, and keep it combed: devotion inside ordinary life.
games.why: the Gurus taught householders to live in the world; uncut and tended, the hair says so every day.

practice: Picture tidying one small thing near you, a drawer, your desk, the kitchen counter, your phone's home screen, slowly, like a comb: nothing thrown out in a rush, just untangling and putting things back where they belong.
Then turn that same gentle comb toward your mind, and let one tangled thought loosen.
